sources.title: 2025 UK greenhouse gas emissions: provisional figures - statistical release
2025 UK greenhouse gas emissions: provisional figures - methodology summary

guard_patterns.handling: Keep UK territorial/TES and memo-item boundaries explicit.
Keep Energy Trends, EEP and DESNZ proxy methods explicit.
Keep CO2e, source-sector, fuel and quarter bases explicit.
Keep 2024 final baseline and 2025 provisional year distinct.
Retain DESNZ Accredited Official Statistics context.
Do not convert national/sector statistics into site or parcel measurements.
Never infer a parcel emission value from these statistics.
Require explicit PASS review for each generated control.

packages.title: 2025 provisional GHG territorial scope and revision QA
facts: 2025 estimates are provisional UK territorial greenhouse gas emissions, meaning emissions occurring within UK borders.
The provisional estimates are subject to revision when final 2025 estimates are published in February 2027.
Data for 1990-2024 are consistent with the 2024 final UK greenhouse gas emissions statistics.
2025 provisional estimates do not follow the same full methodology as final inventory estimates.
Only UK emissions are included; Crown Dependencies and Overseas Territories are not included in the provisional estimates.
Provisional statistics are reported by high-level Territorial Emissions Statistics sectors and fuel type.
Quarterly greenhouse gas emissions estimates are included for years from 2008 onwards.
Temperature-adjusted greenhouse gas emissions are included for years from 2008 onwards.
UK-based international aviation and shipping emissions are shown separately and are not included in UK greenhouse gas totals.
Provisional estimates are not used for formal reporting of performance against UK emissions-reduction targets.

packages.title: 2025 provisional GHG Energy Trends scaling QA
facts: Most provisional energy-use greenhouse gas emissions are estimated using provisional Energy Trends energy statistics.
Energy-use emissions derived from energy data represented 77% of total greenhouse gas emissions based on the 2024 final statistics.
The method assumes the percentage change in emissions between the latest two years matches the percentage change in corresponding energy use.
Year-on-year growth factors are applied to the latest final emissions estimate for each activity and fuel type.
The closest corresponding Energy Trends sector and fuel series is used for the scaling factor.
Quarterly energy-use emissions are allocated in proportion to quarterly energy statistics.
The same sector and fuel data series used for the annual provisional estimate is used for quarterly allocation.
A 5% reduction in gas used in power stations is treated as a 5% reduction in emissions from that gas use in the published methodology example.
Energy-use scaling is a proxy method for the provisional year rather than the full final-inventory method.
Energy Trends and the provisional greenhouse gas release are published together to support this estimation approach.

packages.title: 2025 provisional GHG 29-group fuel scaling QA
facts: Energy-use greenhouse gas emissions are categorised into 29 groups for provisional scaling.
Each group is defined by a greenhouse gas emissions category and fuel.
A scaling factor is calculated from Energy Trends energy-use statistics for each group.
Scaling factors are applied to emissions allocated to each group to derive provisional estimates.
Power-station groups include coal, non-bio waste and gas.
Industry groups include other solid fuels, coal, blast furnace gas, coke oven gas and gas.
Residential-building groups include gas, coal, oil and other solid fuels.
Transport groups include gas, aviation fuel, DERV, motor spirit, LPG, gas oil, coal and fuel oil.
Marine bunkers oil is one of the listed energy-use groups.
The grouped-fuel method is designed to align provisional energy-use changes with emissions estimates.

packages.title: 2025 provisional energy-use held-constant QA
facts: A small number of energy-use greenhouse gas emissions are held constant from the previous year in provisional estimates.
This treatment is used where no suitable Energy Trends data are available for scaling.
Held-constant energy-use emissions represented about 1% of total greenhouse gas emissions based on the 2024 final statistics.
For held-constant activities and fuel types, the provisional annual estimate equals the previous year's final estimate.
No year-on-year change is assumed for these held-constant emissions.
Held-constant annual emissions are allocated equally across the four quarters.
Petrol use in house and garden machinery is an example of energy-use emissions held constant.
The held-constant method is distinct from energy-use emissions scaled with Energy Trends.
The method avoids inventing an unsupported proxy when suitable energy data are unavailable.
These provisional held-constant values remain subject to revision in the final greenhouse gas inventory.

packages.title: 2025 provisional non-energy EEP projection QA
facts: Non-energy-use greenhouse gas emissions made up about 22% of total UK greenhouse gas emissions based on the 2024 final statistics.
Most non-energy-use provisional emissions are estimated using the latest Energy and Emissions Projections (EEP).
Projected non-energy emissions represented about 20% of total UK greenhouse gas emissions based on the 2024 final statistics.
For each category and gas, a growth factor is applied to the previous year's final emissions total.
The growth factor is based on the year-on-year change forecast for that category and gas in the latest EEP.
The reference scenario in the latest EEP is used to derive projected percentage changes.
The method assumes the emissions percentage change matches the EEP projected percentage change for the corresponding category and gas.
A projected 1% fall in methane from agricultural soils is treated as a 1% fall in that provisional emissions category in the methodology example.
Agriculture, waste, LULUCF and other buildings and product uses are largely derived from projections.
These projection-heavy sector totals are marked as estimates because they are less reliable than sectors driven mainly by energy data.

packages.title: 2025 provisional non-energy held-constant QA
facts: A small number of non-energy-use greenhouse gas emissions are held constant from the previous year.
This treatment is used where non-energy emissions are not separated from energy-use emissions in the proxy projections.
Held-constant non-energy emissions represented about 9% of non-energy-related greenhouse gas emissions based on 2024 final statistics.
They represented about 2% of total greenhouse gas emissions based on the 2024 final statistics.
Fugitive greenhouse gas emissions in the fuel-supply sector are the most significant sources in this held-constant category.
For held-constant categories, the provisional estimate equals the previous year's final estimate.
No year-on-year change is assumed for these held-constant non-energy emissions.
These annual emissions are allocated equally between the four quarters.
The held-constant non-energy method is distinct from EEP-derived projection growth factors.
Final inventory publication can revise these provisional held-constant estimates.

packages.title: 2025 provisional GHG gas-by-method mix QA
facts: Carbon dioxide is estimated overwhelmingly from energy-use data in the provisional method: 98% based on the 2024 final mix.
Methane is estimated predominantly from non-energy projections: 89% based on the 2024 final mix.
Nitrous oxide is estimated predominantly from non-energy projections: 91% based on the 2024 final mix.
Hydrofluorocarbon provisional emissions are 100% derived from non-energy projections in the published method table.
Perfluorocarbon provisional emissions are 100% derived from non-energy projections in the published method table.
Sulphur hexafluoride provisional emissions are 100% derived from non-energy projections in the published method table.
Nitrogen trifluoride provisional emissions are 100% derived from non-energy projections in the published method table.
Methane also has smaller energy-derived, energy-held-constant and non-energy-held-constant shares.
Nitrous oxide also has smaller energy-derived and energy-held-constant shares.
Across all gases, the published method mix is 77% energy-derived, 1% energy-held-constant, 20% projection-derived and 2% non-energy-held-constant.

packages.title: 2025 provisional GHG temperature-adjustment QA
facts: Temperature-adjusted emissions are intended to remove the effect of external temperature variation.
Heating degree days are used to quantify deviations from the long-term average.
Heating degree days use a base temperature of 15.5 degrees Celsius in the published methodology.
Temperature adjustments apply only to activities and fuel types with a demonstrated temperature relationship.
A linear regression is fitted between emissions and heating degree days using data from 2002 to 2019.
Later years are excluded from that regression because of behavioural changes during the COVID-19 pandemic.
R-squared is used to assess the strength of the relationship between emissions and heating degree days.
Adjustment is applied only when the regression coefficient is statistically significant and R-squared is sufficiently high.
The long-term average used for the adjustment is the 1991-2020 thirty-year period.
The adjustment removes between-year temperature effects but does not remove normal within-year seasonal variation.

packages.title: 2025 provisional international aviation and shipping bunkers QA
facts: International aviation and shipping emissions are estimated from refuelling from bunkers at UK airports and ports.
These bunker estimates cover refuelling by UK and non-UK operators.
Under UNFCCC reporting guidelines, these emissions are not included in UK national emissions totals.
They are reported as memo items in national greenhouse gas inventories.
They are shown in a separate table from UK territorial greenhouse gas emissions.
Provisional UK-based international aviation and shipping bunker estimates were first included with provisional 2022 estimates.
The provisional bunker method follows the same energy-use scaling approach used for UK provisional energy emissions.
International shipping uses marine-bunkers Energy Trends estimates.
International aviation uses aviation-fuel estimates, the large majority of which relate to international aviation.
Quarterly and temperature-adjusted estimates are not produced for these international aviation and shipping emissions.

packages.title: 2025 provisional electricity-supply coal-zero QA
facts: Electricity-supply emissions come from fuel combustion in power stations for electricity generation.
Electricity supply was provisionally estimated to account for 10% of UK emissions in 2025.
Carbon dioxide accounted for 98% of electricity-supply emissions in 2025.
Electricity-supply emissions fell by 1% between 2024 and 2025.
Coal emissions in the electricity-supply sector fell to zero in 2025 after closure of the UK's last coal-powered station in September 2024.
Total electricity generation was 2% higher in 2025 than in 2024.
Net electricity imports fell 11% from the record high in 2024.
Electricity-supply emissions from gas use increased by 5% in 2025 compared with 2024.
Electricity-supply emissions decreased by 82% between 1990 and 2025.
Nuclear and renewables accounted for a record-high 65% of fuel used for electricity generation in 2025.

packages.title: 2025 provisional fuel-supply sector QA
facts: Fuel-supply emissions arise during production and supply of fuels.
The sector includes combustion in oil refineries and at oil and gas platforms.
The sector includes flaring and venting of gas from oil and gas facilities.
The sector includes leakages from the gas network and methane emissions from coal mining.
Fuel supply accounted for 7% of UK emissions in 2025.
Most fuel-supply emissions in 2025 were from oil and gas supply.
Carbon dioxide accounted for 82% of fuel-supply emissions in 2025.
Fuel-supply emissions decreased by 5% between 2024 and 2025.
The 2024-to-2025 fall was largely due to reduced oil and gas supply combustion.
Fuel-supply emissions decreased by 65% between 1990 and 2025.

packages.title: 2025 provisional domestic-transport sector QA
facts: Domestic transport includes road vehicles, domestic aviation and shipping, fishing vessels and railways.
Domestic transport does not include international aviation or international shipping emissions.
The sector also includes military domestic aviation and shipping within the published definition.
Domestic transport accounted for 31% of all UK emissions in 2025.
Carbon dioxide accounted for 98% of domestic-transport emissions in 2025.
The main source is petrol and diesel use in road vehicles.
Domestic-transport emissions increased by 2% between 2024 and 2025.
The increase was largely due to increased petrol and diesel use in road transport.
Domestic-transport emissions decreased by 9% between 1990 and 2025.
2025 domestic-transport emissions were estimated to be 8% below 2019, the last pre-pandemic year.

packages.title: 2025 provisional buildings source-boundary QA
facts: Buildings and product uses primarily includes fuel combustion in buildings for heating and cooking.
The sector also includes direct product-use emissions from refrigeration and air conditioning.
It also includes garden machinery, anaesthetics, metered-dose inhalers and aerosols.
Buildings and product uses accounted for an estimated 22% of UK emissions in 2025.
Residential fuel combustion accounted for 66% of emissions within the sector.
Commercial buildings accounted for 16% and public-sector buildings 11% of sector emissions.
Other buildings and product uses accounted for the remaining 6% of sector emissions.
TES sector estimates are reported on a source basis.
Electricity-use emissions in buildings are attributed to power stations and therefore the electricity-supply sector rather than buildings.
Buildings and product-use emissions fell by 2% between 2024 and 2025 and are influenced by external temperatures.

packages.title: 2025 provisional industry blast-furnace QA
facts: Industry includes fuel combustion at industrial sites and in industrial machinery.
Industry also includes emissions from industrial processes.
Industrial F-gas emissions such as from refrigeration systems are included in the industry sector.
Industry was estimated to account for 11% of UK emissions in 2025.
Carbon dioxide accounted for 97% of industry emissions in 2025.
Industry emissions fell by 12% between 2024 and 2025.
The fall was largely due to blast-furnace closures in iron and steel and reduced gas use across industries.
Industry emissions decreased by 74% between 1990 and 2025.
Coke-production emissions are included in industry rather than fuel supply in the TES definitions.
Industrial autogeneration emissions remain in industry even when electricity is exported to the grid or heat is used in heat networks.

packages.title: 2025 provisional agriculture waste LULUCF scope QA
facts: Most emissions from agriculture, waste and LULUCF are not related to energy use.
Most provisional emissions for these sectors cannot therefore be derived from provisional energy statistics.
Non-energy emissions in these sectors are largely assumed to change in line with the latest projections.
Combined provisional emissions from agriculture, waste and LULUCF fell by 1%, or about 1 MtCO2e, between 2024 and 2025.
Agriculture includes livestock enteric fermentation, manure management and agricultural soils as well as machinery and fuel combustion.
Agricultural carbon-stock changes are excluded from agriculture and included in LULUCF.
Waste includes landfill, composting, incineration without energy recovery and wastewater handling.
Energy-from-waste incinerator emissions are excluded from waste and reported in electricity supply.
LULUCF includes net CO2 emissions from carbon-stock changes across land categories and harvested wood products.
Biogenic CO2 from activities such as burning biomass for energy is excluded from other sectors to avoid double counting with LULUCF carbon-stock accounting.
